definition: District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008) is a U.S. Supreme Court case holding that the Second Amendment of the United States Constitution protects an individual’s right to possess a firearm unconnected with their service in a militia, including for traditionally lawful purposes such as self-defense in the home. In this case, a police officer who was authorized to carry a handgun while on duty had applied for a registration certificate to lawfully keep a handgun in his home. The District of Columbia (D.C.) rejected the application. The District of Columbia had effectively banned the personal possession of handguns with a prohibition on registering handguns, and the criminalization of carrying an unregistered handgun. Heller sued the District of Columbia on Second Amendment grounds to enjoin the prohibition on handgun registration, the licensing requirement insofar as it prohibited carrying an unlicensed handgun in the home, and the requirements for guns to be locked and disassembled in the home. At the District Court level, the complaint was dismissed, but the District of Columbia Circuit Court of Appeals reversed. The primary issues in Heller were whether the Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess and carry firearms independent of militia service, and whether the District of Columbia's restrictions on handgun possession and firearm storage violated that right. Justice Scalia, writing for a 5-4 majority, split the text of the Second Amendment into two parts. The prefatory clause, “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State” and the operative clause “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.” Justice Scalia first conducted a textual analysis of the operative clause. The phrase “right of the people” appears in some form three times in the Constitution. In each instance, the rights are individual rights, not “collective rights” that may only be exercised by participation in a group.
